title: Azure Solutions Architect (AZ-305)
tagline: Designing infrastructure, data, and integration solutions
disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Microsoft. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original; no exam content is reproduced.

scenarios.title: The acquisition's identities
scenarios.situation: Contoso acquires Fabrikam. Two Entra tenants must collaborate immediately, but Contoso's CISO won't merge directories for a year.
scenarios.prompt: What identity design enables secure cross-tenant collaboration now?
choices: Cross-tenant access with B2B collaboration, scoped Conditional Access, and access packages
Merging both tenants this weekend
Sharing one global admin account
Federating both tenants to a third IdP without Entra
scenarios.why: Entra's cross-tenant access settings plus B2B collaboration let users from one tenant access the other's resources under explicit trust, Conditional Access, and MFA requirements — the architected path for M&A collaboration without a directory merge.
scenarios.hint: Which Entra feature is built for 'their users, our resources' without merging directories?

scenarios.title: Standing admin rights
scenarios.situation: Sixty engineers hold permanent Global Administrator. An audit flags this as the company's top identity risk.
scenarios.prompt: What design removes standing privilege while keeping emergency access possible?
choices: Privileged Identity Management: eligible (not active) assignments, MFA-gated activation, approval, and time-bound access
Deleting all admin accounts
Giving everyone Global Admin so it's 'equal'
Weekly password rotations for admins
scenarios.why: PIM implements just-in-time administration: admins hold eligible assignments and activate the role only when needed, with MFA, approval workflows, justification, and automatic expiry. This eliminates standing privilege — the core of identity security design.
scenarios.hint: How do you give someone admin power only for the hour they need it?

scenarios.title: The connection string leak
scenarios.situation: An app's SQL connection string with username and password was committed to a public GitHub repo. The architect wants credentials eliminated from code entirely.
scenarios.prompt: What design removes secrets from the application?
choices: Managed identity — the app authenticates to Azure SQL as its own identity with no stored credentials
A longer password rotated monthly
Storing the password in appsettings.json with restricted file permissions
Using the same credential across all environments
scenarios.why: Managed identities give Azure resources an Entra identity; the platform handles credential rotation invisibly. Apps use DefaultAzureCredential-style flows to get tokens — no passwords in code, config, or vaults to leak. (Key Vault is for secrets you truly must keep, like third-party API keys.)
scenarios.hint: What identity type means the app never holds a password at all?

scenarios.title: The third-party API key
scenarios.situation: An app needs a third-party payment API key — a secret that can't be replaced by a managed identity.
scenarios.prompt: Where should this secret live, and how should the app read it?
choices: Azure Key Vault with a private endpoint; the app authenticates via its managed identity and reads the secret at runtime
In the source code repository
In an environment variable on the developer's laptop
In a storage account blob with a SAS token
scenarios.why: Key Vault is the designed home for secrets, keys, and certificates: RBAC-scoped access, private endpoint networking, rotation, and audit logging. The app's managed identity is granted Get on secrets only — no human ever sees the value.
scenarios.hint: Secrets you must keep go in the vault; how does the app prove who it is to the vault?

scenarios.title: The flat network
scenarios.situation: A startup's Azure footprint is one giant VNet where every workload talks to every other. A breach in the marketing site reached the payment database.
scenarios.prompt: What network security design limits blast radius?
choices: Hub-and-spoke with NSGs, Azure Firewall in the hub, and private endpoints for PaaS — segmenting tiers
A bigger single VNet
Public endpoints on all PaaS for easier access
Removing all NSGs for performance
scenarios.why: Hub-and-spoke segments workloads into isolated spokes with the hub hosting shared security (Azure Firewall for egress filtering, Bastion, VPN/ExpressRoute). NSGs and private endpoints add per-tier controls so one compromised tier can't reach the others.
scenarios.hint: How do you stop lateral movement between tiers by design?

scenarios.title: The subscription sprawl
scenarios.situation: A company creates subscriptions ad hoc — no consistent policies, no network standards, no cost tagging. Audits keep failing.
choices: A landing-zone design: management group hierarchy, baseline policies, hub networking, and identity foundation applied consistently
One subscription for everything
Letting each team invent its own standards
Deleting old subscriptions quarterly
scenarios.why: Landing zones (Cloud Adoption Framework) provide the repeatable foundation: management groups for policy/RBAC inheritance, connectivity hub, identity baseline, and guardrails — so every workload subscription starts compliant instead of drifting.
scenarios.hint: What framework gives every new subscription the same secure starting point?

scenarios.title: The lift-and-shift database
scenarios.situation: A legacy app needs SQL Server Agent jobs, cross-database queries, and near-100% compatibility with on-premises SQL Server, but the company wants PaaS management.
choices: Azure SQL Managed Instance — near-full SQL Server compatibility as a PaaS
Azure SQL Database single database — some features like Agent unavailable
SQL Server on Azure VMs — IaaS, full control but self-managed
Azure Cosmos DB
scenarios.why: SQL Managed Instance offers near-100% compatibility with on-premises SQL Server (Agent jobs, cross-db queries, CLR) while Microsoft manages patching and HA. Single databases suit cloud-native apps; VMs suit when OS-level control is required.
scenarios.hint: Which PaaS keeps SQL Agent and cross-database queries working?

scenarios.title: The global shopping cart
scenarios.situation: A retailer's cart service needs single-digit-millisecond reads/writes for users on five continents, with automatic failover.
scenarios.prompt: Which data store is designed for this?
choices: Azure Cosmos DB with multi-region writes — global distribution with tunable consistency
Azure SQL Database in one region
Azure Table storage in one region
SQL Server on a VM with replication
scenarios.why: Cosmos DB is built for globally distributed NoSQL: multi-region writes, 99.999% SLA options, and five tunable consistency levels trading freshness for latency. Regional relational databases can't match the global latency profile.
scenarios.hint: Millisecond global access with automatic failover — which store is purpose-built?

scenarios.title: The lakehouse
scenarios.situation: Analysts need SQL over the data lake's Parquet files today, and data scientists need Spark over the same files tomorrow — without duplicating data.
scenarios.prompt: What design serves both engines from one copy?
choices: Open formats (Parquet/Delta Lake) on ADLS Gen2 queried by Synapse serverless SQL and Spark pools
Copying data into a SQL database and a separate Spark cluster
CSV files on a file share
Two separate data lakes
scenarios.why: Storing data once in open formats (Parquet, Delta Lake) on ADLS Gen2 lets Synapse serverless SQL pools query it with T-SQL and Spark pools process it — the lakehouse pattern. Delta Lake adds ACID transactions and time travel on top.
scenarios.hint: One copy of data, two engines. What storage format makes that possible?

scenarios.title: The hot partition
scenarios.situation: A Cosmos DB container with 2 TB of data throttles constantly. All documents share one partition key value — the tenant ID of the largest customer.
evidence: 429 rate-limited requests: 38% | normalized RU consumption on partition 7: 100%
choices: A hot partition — the partition key doesn't distribute throughput; choose a high-cardinality key aligned with query patterns
Cosmos DB can't handle 2 TB
Throughput should be set to manual minimum
The container needs a second region
scenarios.why: Partition key choice is the most consequential Cosmos DB design decision: it must distribute both data and request volume evenly and match query patterns. A single hot value concentrates all RU consumption on one physical partition — throttling regardless of provisioned throughput.
scenarios.hint: All traffic hits one partition. What design decision caused that?

scenarios.title: The compliance retention
scenarios.situation: A bank must retain database backups for 7 years and be able to restore to any point in the last 30 days.
choices: Long-term retention (LTR) policies for the 7-year requirement plus point-in-time restore for the 30-day window
Weekly manual exports to a laptop
Geo-replication alone
Relying on the default 7-day retention
scenarios.why: Azure SQL's automated backups give point-in-time restore (7–35 days configurable); long-term retention policies keep full backups in RA-GRS storage for up to 10 years. The two mechanisms cover different requirements — recency vs. compliance archive.
scenarios.hint: Which two backup features cover 'any point in 30 days' versus 'keep for 7 years'?

scenarios.title: The mixed workload
scenarios.situation: An architect must store: user sessions (key-value, ephemeral), product catalog (flexible documents), and financial transactions (strict ACID).
scenarios.prompt: What is the sound design approach?
choices: Polyglot persistence — the right store per workload (cache, document DB, relational) rather than one store for all
One relational database for everything
One document database for everything
Flat files for everything
scenarios.why: Polyglot persistence matches each workload to its ideal store: ephemeral sessions in a cache (Redis), flexible catalog in a document DB, transactions in relational. Forcing all three into one store compromises each workload's needs.
scenarios.hint: Three workloads with different shapes and guarantees — one store or three?

scenarios.title: The two numbers
scenarios.situation: Leadership says 'we can't lose more than 15 minutes of orders, and the site must be back within 4 hours of a regional disaster.'
scenarios.prompt: How does the architect translate this?
choices: RPO ≤ 15 minutes (max data loss) drives replication frequency; RTO ≤ 4 hours (max downtime) drives recovery automation and architecture
Both numbers describe the backup schedule
RPO measures downtime; RTO measures data loss
These are SLA percentages in disguise
scenarios.why: RPO (recovery point objective) = how much data loss is tolerable, dictating replication/backup frequency. RTO (recovery time objective) = how long downtime is tolerable, dictating how automated and warm the recovery environment must be. Every BCDR design starts here.
scenarios.hint: Which number is about lost data and which is about downtime?

scenarios.title: The zero-downtime demand
scenarios.situation: A trading platform tolerates essentially zero downtime and zero data loss across a regional outage.
choices: Active-active across regions (e.g., Cosmos DB multi-region writes, Front Door routing) — at the highest cost and complexity
Backup and restore to a second region
A single region with availability zones only
Weekly database exports
scenarios.why: Active-active serves traffic from multiple regions simultaneously with synchronous or near-synchronous replication — the only pattern approaching zero RTO/RPO across regions. It costs the most and demands conflict-resolution design; pilot-light and backup/restore accept longer RTOs for lower cost.
scenarios.hint: Zero downtime across a regional failure demands which recovery pattern?

scenarios.title: The budget-conscious DR
scenarios.situation: A nonprofit needs regional DR but can't afford to run a full duplicate environment 24/7.
choices: Pilot light or warm standby — minimal always-on footprint (replicated data, small core) scaled up on failover
Active-active
No DR at all
Running everything twice at full size
scenarios.why: Pilot light keeps the minimum viable footprint running (data replication, core services) and scales out during failover — balancing RTO against cost. It's the standard answer when active-active is unaffordable but backup/restore RTOs are too slow.
scenarios.hint: Minimal always-on, scale up on disaster — which pattern is that?

scenarios.title: Files vs failover
scenarios.situation: A team confuses Azure Backup with Azure Site Recovery, proposing Site Recovery to restore a single deleted file.
choices: Azure Backup protects data (files, VMs, databases) for restore; Site Recovery replicates whole workloads for failover to a second site
They are the same service
Site Recovery backs up files; Backup fails over VMs
Neither handles on-premises workloads
scenarios.why: Backup = data protection and granular restore (a file, a database point-in-time). Site Recovery = workload replication and orchestrated failover/failback of entire VMs and apps to a secondary region. Different problems, different tools.
scenarios.hint: Granular restore versus whole-workload failover — which service does each?

scenarios.title: The regional outage
scenarios.situation: An app spread across availability zones in East US survives datacenter failures, but leadership asks about a full East US regional outage.
choices: Cross-region replication/failover (paired region, Traffic Manager/Front Door) — zones don't survive regional loss
More zones in the same region
Bigger VMs in the same zones
A second VNet in East US
scenarios.why: Availability zones protect against datacenter-level failure within a region; only cross-region architecture (replication + global load balancing + failover runbooks) survives a regional event. Zones and regions are different tiers of resilience.
scenarios.hint: Zones are in-region. What tier of resilience covers losing the whole region?

scenarios.title: The untested backup
scenarios.situation: A company has backups running for two years but has never attempted a restore. An auditor asks for proof of recoverability.
choices: Regular restore testing and documented runbooks — backups are worthless until a restore is proven
Longer retention
More frequent backups
A second backup vault in the same region
scenarios.why: An untested backup is a hope, not a plan. Mature BCDR designs schedule restore drills, document RTO/RPO validation, and keep runbooks current — auditors specifically look for evidence of tested recovery, not just backup jobs succeeding.
scenarios.hint: What proves a backup actually works?

scenarios.title: The batch genome job
scenarios.situation: A research team runs a 6-hour parallel genome analysis once a week — no steady load, massive burst compute, then nothing.
choices: Azure Batch or VMSS with autoscale-to-zero / spot — pay only for burst hours
Always-on VMs sized for peak
App Service with Always On
A single container instance running 24/7
scenarios.why: Episodic parallel HPC workloads fit Azure Batch (job scheduling across pooled VMs, including spot) or scale sets that scale to zero — you pay for 6 hours, not 168. Always-on infrastructure for weekly bursts is pure waste.
scenarios.hint: Six hours a week of massive parallelism — what compute pattern avoids paying for idle time?

scenarios.title: The microservices call
scenarios.situation: A team runs 12 microservices, wants Kubernetes API compatibility for their GitOps tooling, and needs node-level control for GPU workloads.
choices: Azure Kubernetes Service — full Kubernetes control including node pools and GPUs
Azure Container Apps — serverless containers without Kubernetes API access
Container Instances — single containers, no orchestration
App Service — not container orchestration
scenarios.why: AKS provides managed Kubernetes with full API access, custom node pools (including GPU SKUs), and GitOps integration. Container Apps is excellent for serverless microservices but abstracts the Kubernetes layer away — wrong when the team needs node control and K8s-native tooling.
scenarios.hint: They need the Kubernetes API and GPU node pools. Which service gives both?

scenarios.title: The factory servers
scenarios.situation: A manufacturer has 300 Windows servers on factory floors that can't move to Azure, but IT wants unified policy, monitoring, and patching from Azure.
scenarios.prompt: What extends Azure management to them?
choices: Azure Arc — projects on-premises/edge servers into Azure Resource Manager for policy, monitoring, and extensions
ExpressRoute alone
Migrating them all to Azure VMs
A site-to-site VPN
scenarios.why: Azure Arc-enabled servers bring non-Azure machines under ARM: Azure Policy guest configuration, Monitor, Defender, and Update Manager work uniformly. It's the hybrid management answer when migration isn't possible.
scenarios.hint: How do you manage servers you can't migrate as if they were Azure resources?

scenarios.title: The TLS termination
scenarios.situation: A global web app needs TLS termination, WAF protection, and routing to regional backends with the lowest-latency choice per user.
choices: Azure Front Door — global anycast entry, WAF, TLS termination, latency-based routing to origins
Application Gateway — regional only
Azure Firewall — not a reverse proxy/WAF for HTTP
Traffic Manager — DNS-based, no TLS termination or WAF
scenarios.why: Front Door is the global (multi-region) HTTP entry point: anycast, WAF integration, TLS offload, and latency-based routing. Application Gateway is the regional equivalent; Traffic Manager is DNS-level without HTTP features.
scenarios.hint: Global entry + WAF + TLS + latency routing — which service combines all four?

scenarios.title: The video pipeline
scenarios.situation: A media pipeline ingests 50 TB/day of video, processes it with Spark, and serves thumbnails worldwide with low latency.
choices: ADLS Gen2 (hierarchical namespace, Spark-optimized) for ingest/process, plus Azure CDN or Front Door caching for global thumbnail delivery
Premium SSD managed disks for 50 TB/day ingest
Archive tier for active processing
A single file share for everything
scenarios.why: ADLS Gen2 is the analytics-optimized object store (hierarchical namespace, fine-grained ACLs, Spark/Hadoop compatible); CDN/Front Door caches hot thumbnails at the edge. Managed disks are VM-attached block storage — wrong for shared analytics at this scale.
scenarios.hint: Shared analytics-scale ingest plus global low-latency reads — which two services?

scenarios.title: The review framework
scenarios.situation: An architect is asked to systematically review a workload design before production — reliability, security, cost, operations, performance.
choices: The Azure Well-Architected Framework — five pillars with assessment reviews
The Cloud Adoption Framework — migration-focused
Azure Policy — enforcement, not design review
The pricing calculator
scenarios.why: The Well-Architected Framework's five pillars (Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence, Performance Efficiency) plus the Well-Architected Review tooling give a structured design assessment. CAF covers cloud adoption strategy; WAF covers workload quality.
scenarios.hint: Which framework's pillars are reliability, security, cost, operations, and performance?

scenarios.title: The partner API
scenarios.situation: A company must expose internal APIs to partners with rate limits, API keys, usage analytics, and a developer portal — without rewriting the backends.
choices: Azure API Management — gateway policies, subscriptions/keys, throttling, analytics, developer portal
A raw Azure Function URL per API
An NSG in front of the backend
Application Gateway alone
scenarios.why: API Management is the full-lifecycle API gateway: policy enforcement (rate limits, transformation, auth), product/subscription key management, analytics, and a self-service developer portal — the designed facade for partner exposure.
scenarios.hint: Rate limits, keys, portal, analytics over existing backends — which service?

scenarios.title: Orders vs telemetry
scenarios.situation: The architect must choose messaging for: (a) order processing requiring exactly-once, ordered, transactional delivery; (b) 1M/sec device telemetry fan-out.
choices: Service Bus for orders (queues, transactions, ordering); Event Hubs for telemetry (high-throughput streaming ingestion)
Event Hubs for orders; Service Bus for telemetry
Event Grid for both
Storage queues for both
scenarios.why: Service Bus = enterprise messaging (queues/topics, transactions, sessions/ordering, dead-lettering) for orders. Event Hubs = big-data streaming ingestion (millions of events/sec, partitions, consumer groups) for telemetry. Event Grid = event routing for reactive scenarios — a third distinct pattern.
scenarios.hint: Transactional ordered delivery versus massive streaming fan-out — which service per workload?

scenarios.title: The blob-triggered workflow
scenarios.situation: When a file lands in Blob storage, three independent downstream systems must react — a function, a logic app, and a webhook.
choices: Event Grid — pub/sub event routing with multiple subscribers per event
Event Hubs — streaming ingestion, overkill for discrete events
Service Bus — messaging, not event fan-out
A timer-triggered function polling the container
scenarios.why: Event Grid routes discrete events (like BlobCreated) to multiple subscribers with push delivery and filtering — the reactive integration pattern. Polling wastes resources; streaming platforms suit continuous data, not discrete notifications.
scenarios.hint: One event, three independent reactions. Which service is pub/sub event routing?

scenarios.title: The SaaS approval flow
scenarios.situation: HR needs: when a ServiceNow ticket closes, post to Teams, wait for manager approval, then create an Entra account. Built by a non-developer team.
choices: Logic Apps — visual workflow designer with 1000+ connectors (ServiceNow, Teams, Entra) for citizen integrators
Azure Functions — code-first, wrong for a non-developer team
A VM running scripts
Event Hubs
scenarios.why: Logic Apps' designer and connector ecosystem make human-in-the-loop SaaS workflows buildable without code. Functions suit code-first compute; the scenario's approval step and connector breadth point to Logic Apps.
scenarios.hint: Visual workflow, SaaS connectors, human approval, non-developer builders — which tool?

scenarios.title: The locked-down integration
scenarios.situation: APIM must call backend Functions and SQL with no traffic traversing the public internet, per a regulatory requirement.
choices: Private endpoints for APIM/Functions/SQL on the VNet (Premium/isolated tiers as needed) plus private DNS
Public endpoints with IP whitelisting
Service endpoints only — the PaaS public endpoints remain
A VPN from APIM to the backends
scenarios.why: Private endpoints bring each PaaS into the VNet with private IPs, so integration traffic never leaves the private network. Note tier implications: APIM needs Premium (or Standard v2) for VNet injection/private endpoints — a real design constraint.
scenarios.hint: Regulation says no public internet for integration traffic. Which construct privatizes PaaS?

scenarios.title: The distributed order
scenarios.situation: An order flow spans inventory service, payment service, and shipping service — each with its own database. A payment failure must undo the inventory reservation.
choices: Saga pattern — orchestrated or choreographed compensating transactions across services
A distributed two-phase commit across databases
A single shared database for all services
Ignoring the failure and shipping anyway
scenarios.why: Microservices can't share ACID transactions across databases; the saga pattern sequences local transactions with compensating actions (cancel reservation) on failure. Two-phase commit doesn't scale across autonomous services.
scenarios.hint: No shared database, but failures must roll back prior steps. Which pattern?

scenarios.title: The unknown estate
scenarios.situation: A company wants to migrate 400 VMs to Azure but doesn't know their utilization, dependencies, or readiness.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first step?
choices: Azure Migrate assessment — agentless discovery, dependency mapping, utilization analysis, and right-sizing recommendations
Migrating the VMs immediately
Buying reserved instances first
Asking each team to guess their usage
scenarios.why: Azure Migrate's discovery and assessment phase maps dependencies, measures actual utilization, and produces right-sized Azure targets with cost estimates — the evidence base for every migration wave plan. Migrating blind guarantees waste and outages.
scenarios.hint: Before moving 400 VMs, what produces the dependency map and right-sizing data?

scenarios.title: The strategy choice
scenarios.situation: For each app in the portfolio, the team must pick: rehost, refactor, rearchitect, rebuild, replace, or retire.
choices: The 6 R's of migration strategy — matching each workload to the right transformation depth
The 5 pillars of WAF
The 3 service models
A licensing audit
scenarios.why: The 6 Rs (rehost/lift-and-shift, refactor, rearchitect, rebuild, replace with SaaS, retire) force an explicit strategy per app instead of one-size-fits-all. Rehost is fastest; replace/retire often deliver the best economics.
scenarios.hint: Which framework assigns each app a migration strategy?

scenarios.title: The database move
scenarios.situation: A 4 TB on-premises SQL Server must move to Azure SQL Managed Instance with minimal downtime during cutover.
choices: Azure Database Migration Service / MI link with continuous replication and a planned cutover
Backup-and-restore over a weekend outage
Detaching MDF files and copying them
Rewriting the app for Cosmos DB first
scenarios.why: Online migration (DMS or the MI link feature) replicates continuously and cuts over with minutes of downtime — the minimal-downtime pattern for large databases. Offline backup/restore means the outage lasts as long as the 4 TB transfer.
scenarios.hint: Minimal downtime for a 4 TB database move — which migration mode?

scenarios.title: The dependency order
scenarios.situation: Assessment shows the web tier depends on an app tier that depends on a database. The team wants to migrate the web tier first.
scenarios.prompt: What does the wave plan say?
choices: Migrate in dependency order (database → app → web) or as a wave group — migrating dependents first strands them
Migrate in any order; dependencies resolve automatically
Migrate the web tier first for quick wins
Skip the database entirely
scenarios.why: Wave planning groups apps by dependency: migrate dependencies first (or together in one wave) so nothing lands in Azure pointing at a database still on-premises. The dependency map from assessment drives the wave sequence.
scenarios.hint: The web tier needs the app tier needs the database. What order do waves follow?

scenarios.title: The split-brain DNS
scenarios.situation: During migration, some VMs are on-premises and some in Azure, and name resolution breaks for the migrated ones.
choices: Hybrid DNS — conditional forwarders / private resolver so both environments resolve each other's names
More bandwidth
Bigger VMs
A second ExpressRoute
scenarios.why: Coexistence requires name resolution both ways: on-premises DNS forwarding Azure private zones (via Azure Private DNS Resolver or forwarders) and Azure resolving on-premises names. DNS is the most common hybrid migration breakage.
scenarios.hint: Migrated and unmigrated servers can't find each other by name. Which design piece is missing?

scenarios.title: The migration foundation
scenarios.situation: The team is ready to migrate but has no Azure footprint: no subscriptions structure, no hub network, no baseline policies.
scenarios.prompt: What comes before the first workload migration?
choices: Build the landing zone first — management groups, connectivity, identity, and guardrails — then migrate into it
Migrate one app to learn, then design the foundation
Use the default subscription as-is
Skip governance for speed
scenarios.why: CAF's ready phase: establish the landing zone (subscriptions, networking, identity, governance) before migrating workloads. Migrating into an ungoverned tenant creates the sprawl the migration was supposed to fix.
scenarios.hint: What must exist before the first workload lands?
